# A catalogue of metrics on `f` {#sec-catalogue} Every metric in this chapter has the same signature, `f(idx, ctx) -> scalar`, and every one operates on the molecular coancestry matrix from @sec-coancestry. That uniformity is not tidiness: it is what makes metrics interchangeable inside an optimiser, and it is what lets @sec-choosing benchmark them against each other on equal terms. The chapter also settles the question of what "no loss" means, which turns out to be less obvious than it sounds. ## Group coancestry, and the off-diagonal problem The group coancestry [@cockerham1967] of a set $S$ of $n$ individuals is the mean of **all** $n^2$ elements, diagonal included: $$\theta_S \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\sum_{i \in S}\sum_{j \in S} f_{ij} \;=\; \frac{1}{n^2}\,\mathbf{1}'\mathbf{f}_S\mathbf{1}.$$ It is the probability that two alleles sampled at random *from the whole set* are identical -- including the possibility that both come from the same individual. That is why the diagonal enters: it is the chance of sampling the same individual twice, which is entirely real when the set is used as a crossing pool. Splitting the diagonal mean $\bar f_d$ from the off-diagonal mean $\bar f_o$, $$\theta_S \;=\; \frac{\bar f_d}{n} \;+\; \frac{n-1}{n}\,\bar f_o . \tag{1}$$ So the off-diagonal mean -- the metric many programmes already report -- is one of two terms. When $\bar f_d$ varies little across individuals, which is the case in an all-F1 population, the two rank almost identically: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sels <- list(random = sel_random(ctx, n_sel), trunc_cap = sel_truncation_cap(ctx, n_sel), greedy_w1 = sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = 1), greedy_div = sel_greedy(ctx, n_sel, w = 0), truncation = sel_truncation(ctx, n_sel)) cmp <- t(sapply(sels, function(s) c(theta = theta_group(s, ctx), offdiag = mean_offdiag(s, ctx)))) fmt(as.data.frame(cmp), 5) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | theta| offdiag| |:----------|-------:|-------:| |random | 0.67426| 0.67180| |trunc_cap | 0.67522| 0.67280| |greedy_w1 | 0.68759| 0.68539| |greedy_div | 0.66976| 0.66730| |truncation | 0.68759| 0.68539|
::: ```{.r .cell-code} c(rank_correlation = cor(cmp[, "theta"], cmp[, "offdiag"], method = "spearman")) #> rank_correlation #> 1 ``` ::: The off-diagonal metric ranks correctly. What it does not give you is an interpretable scale or a defensible baseline -- which is what the rest of this chapter supplies. ## Gene diversity: $\theta$ and $H_e$ are the same quantity {#sec-identity} This is the result that simplifies everything downstream. Starting from the definition and swapping the order of summation, the double sum factors: $$\frac{1}{n^2}\sum_i\sum_j x_{ik}x_{jk} = \Big(\frac{1}{n}\sum_i x_{ik}\Big)^2 = \bar p_k^2,$$ with $\bar p_k$ the **group's** allele frequency. Hence $$\theta_S = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k \big(\bar p_k^2 + \bar q_k^2\big), \qquad GD_S = 1 - \theta_S = \frac{1}{m}\sum_k 2\,\bar p_k \bar q_k \;\equiv\; H_e,$$ which is exactly Nei's gene diversity [@nei1973]. **Group coancestry and expected heterozygosity are not two independent checks. They are one quantity written two ways.** ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(via_submatrix = theta_group(idx, ctx), via_frequency = theta_from_freq(idx, ctx), difference = theta_group(idx, ctx) - theta_from_freq(idx, ctx)) #> via_submatrix via_frequency difference #> 0.6734562 0.6734562 0.0000000 c(GD = gene_diversity(idx, ctx), He_Nei = he_nei(idx, ctx)) #> GD He_Nei #> 0.3265438 0.3265438 ``` ::: Equality to machine precision is the implementation's strongest sanity check. If it fails, `f` is centered, rescaled, or built on the wrong marker coding. Three practical consequences: 1. One fewer metric to justify to a technical committee. 2. "Losing 5% of diversity" acquires an exact meaning: 5% of the set's expected heterozygosity. 3. Two computation routes with the same answer and very different costs. The matrix route is $O(n^2)$; the frequency route is $O(nm)$. For $n = 200$ and $m = 25000$ that is forty thousand operations against five million. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} reps <- 40 t_mat <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(reps)) theta_group(idx, ctx))[["elapsed"]] t_frq <- system.time(for (i in seq_len(reps)) theta_from_freq(idx, ctx))[["elapsed"]] c(us_matrix = 1e6 * t_mat / reps, us_frequency = 1e6 * t_frq / reps, ratio = t_frq / t_mat) #> us_matrix us_frequency ratio #> 25 150 6 ``` ::: The matrix route is the one that belongs in an optimiser's inner loop. @sec-collapse makes it cheaper still. ## Status number $N_s$ {#sec-ns} @lindgren1997 express group coancestry on the scale of individual counts: $$N_s = \frac{1}{2\theta_S}.$$ $N_s$ is the number of **unrelated, non-inbred** individuals that would have the same gene diversity as the observed set. The edge cases fix the intuition: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fake <- ctx fake$f <- matrix(0.5, 5, 5) # unrelated, p = 0.5 c(theta = theta_group(1:5, fake), Ns = status_number(1:5, fake)) #> theta Ns #> 0.5 1.0 fake$f <- matrix(1, 5, 5) # all identical and homozygous c(theta = theta_group(1:5, fake), Ns = status_number(1:5, fake)) #> theta Ns #> 1.0 0.5 ``` ::: ::: {.callout-warning} ## $N_s$ is a descriptor, not a drift projection @toro2020 show that the **rate-based** effective size $N_e = 1/(2\Delta F)$ loses meaning under molecular diversity management: optimisation increases diversity in early generations, producing a negative $\Delta F$ and therefore a negative $N_e$, with no long-term asymptote. This does not invalidate $N_s$. $N_s$ is a monotonic reparametrisation of $\theta$ -- a *static descriptor of a set* -- while $N_e$ is a *rate between generations*. Use $N_s$ to compare sets; do not extrapolate it to project future drift. For the same reason, do not substitute the linkage-disequilibrium $N_e$ here: that estimates population history, not the composition of a selected sample. ::: And, from @sec-genomic-era: $\theta$ tracks homozygosity, not drift. $GD$ and $N_s$ answer "how much heterozygosity does this selection preserve", which is the right question for next season's hybrid vigour. They do not certify that allele frequencies are moving as unmanaged drift would have moved them, which matters more across multiple recurrent cycles than for a single round of hybrid selection. ## Effective number of parents A metric independent of $\mathbf{f}$, computed purely from the pedigree. With $p_i$ the frequency with which line $i$ appears as a parent among the selected hybrids, $$N_{e(\text{par})} = \frac{1}{\sum_i p_i^2},$$ the inverse Simpson index. It captures precisely what coancestry blurs: a set of 200 hybrids can have an acceptable $\theta$ while drawing on only 12 lines, if those 12 happen to be genetically distant from each other. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} c(sapply(sels, ne_parents, ctx = ctx), theoretical_max = ctx$n_lines) #> random trunc_cap greedy_w1 greedy_div truncation #> 39.34426 31.03448 13.01989 37.30570 13.01989 #> theoretical_max #> 50.00000 ``` ::: Truncation collapses the parent base far more than it moves $\theta$. Its cost is a `tabulate` call, which makes it a natural candidate to enter the objective function alongside $\theta$ -- and in @sec-choosing it does. ## Allelic richness {#sec-richness} $\theta$ and $H_e$ are averages across markers and are dominated by intermediate-frequency alleles. A lost rare allele barely moves them, yet the loss is irreversible. So count markers that were polymorphic in the population and became rare or fixed in the selection: $$A_{\text{lost}} = \#\{k : \text{MAF}^{(S)}_k < 0.05 \;\wedge\; \text{MAF}^{(\text{pop})}_k \ge 0.05\}.$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sapply(sels, alleles_lost, ctx = ctx) #> random trunc_cap greedy_w1 greedy_div truncation #> 24 43 110 22 110 ``` ::: It is the only metric in this catalogue **genuinely non-redundant** with $\theta$ -- a claim @sec-choosing tests rather than asserts. @lopezcortegano2019 compared, in a subdivided simulated population, strategies maximising *expected heterozygosity* ($H_T$, the same family as $GD$) against strategies maximising *allelic diversity* ($A_T$). Maximising $A_T$ retained more alleles **and** controlled molecular inbreeding better than maximising $H_T$. The mechanism connects directly to @sec-genomic-era: heterozygosity-maximising management pushes allele frequencies toward 0.5, which favours rare alleles in the short run but does not stop them drifting to loss once they are no longer the rarest; allele-count management defends every segregating allele directly. Their recommendation for structured conservation programmes was to make $A_T$, not $H_T$, the primary target. In this pipeline's terms: `alleles_lost` deserves a place next to $\theta$ as a *tracked outcome*, not only as a post-hoc sanity check, whenever the selection feeds several future cycles rather than a single hybrid release. ## Distances: E-NE and A-NE With distance $d_{ij} = 1 - f_{ij}$, Core Hunter 3 [@debeukelaer2018] defines two measures capturing opposite aspects that $\theta$ alone cannot separate: $$\text{E-NE} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i \in S} \min_{j \in S,\, j \ne i} d_{ij}, \qquad \text{A-NE} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \min_{j \in S} d_{ij}.$$ - **E-NE**, entry-to-nearest-entry, measures **non-redundancy within the selection**. It distinguishes "200 individuals spread out" from "100 near-identical pairs spread out" -- configurations that can share the same $\theta$. - **A-NE**, accession-to-nearest-entry, measures **representativeness of the population**. It detects a selection that optimises $\theta$ by concentrating in one region of genetic space and ignoring the rest. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(t(sapply(sels, function(s) c(ENE = ene(s, ctx), ANE = ane(s, ctx)))), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | ENE| ANE| |:----------|------:|------:| |random | 0.2533| 0.2471| |trunc_cap | 0.2536| 0.2561| |greedy_w1 | 0.2527| 0.2523| |greedy_div | 0.2607| 0.2504| |truncation | 0.2527| 0.2523|
::: ::: Note the direction: A-NE is a distance to the *nearest selected entry*, so **lower is better** for representativeness. ## Effective dimensionality Over the eigenvalues of the submatrix, the participation ratio $$D_{\text{eff}} = \frac{(\sum_i \lambda_i)^2}{\sum_i \lambda_i^2}$$ counts how many independent directions of genetic variation remain: 1 if all variation lies on a single axis, $n$ if spread evenly. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(sapply(sels, eff_dim, ctx = ctx), 2) #> random trunc_cap greedy_w1 greedy_div truncation #> 28.59 23.99 12.72 27.92 12.72 ``` ::: The submatrix is **double-centered** before the eigendecomposition. On a raw all-positive `f` the leading eigenvalue is just $n\theta$, so an uncentered version would only re-measure $\theta$ under a more expensive name -- a mistake worth naming because it is easy to make and produces a plausible-looking number. ## Decomposition by heterotic group In hybrid maize the diversity **between** pools is the engine of heterosis and cannot be spent; the diversity **within** each pool is the fuel for future progress. @sec-heterosis derives the first half of that sentence -- `GD_BS` weighted by dominance deviations *is* the divergence half of expected heterosis -- and qualifies it: divergence is worth having where it lands on the dominance loci, and worth nothing where it does not. @sec-cycles demonstrates the second half. Following @caballero2002, compute molecular coancestry between lines and weight it by each line's usage among the selected hybrids: $$\theta_A = \mathbf{w}_A' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_A, \qquad \theta_B = \mathbf{w}_B' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_B, \qquad \theta_{AB} = \mathbf{w}_A' \mathbf{f}^{L} \mathbf{w}_B.$$ ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(t(sapply(sels, theta_pools, ctx = ctx)), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | theta_A| theta_B| theta_AB| |:----------|-------:|-------:|--------:| |random | 0.7090| 0.7095| 0.6393| |trunc_cap | 0.7096| 0.7153| 0.6380| |greedy_w1 | 0.7581| 0.7219| 0.6352| |greedy_div | 0.7053| 0.7066| 0.6336| |truncation | 0.7581| 0.7219| 0.6352|
::: ::: Feeding those into the Caballero & Toro partition of @sec-subdivided: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(t(sapply(sels, gd_partition, ctx = ctx)), 4) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | GD_WI_hyb| GD_T| GD_WI| GD_BI| GD_BS| F_ST| |:----------|---------:|------:|-----:|------:|------:|------:| |random | 0.1801| 0.3257| 0| 0.2907| 0.0350| 0.1074| |trunc_cap | 0.1816| 0.3248| 0| 0.2876| 0.0372| 0.1146| |greedy_w1 | 0.1823| 0.3124| 0| 0.2600| 0.0524| 0.1678| |greedy_div | 0.1853| 0.3302| 0| 0.2941| 0.0361| 0.1095| |truncation | 0.1823| 0.3124| 0| 0.2600| 0.0524| 0.1678|
::: ::: Two things to read here. `GD_WI` is **exactly zero**: the parent lines are inbred, so there is no within-individual diversity at line level -- the algebra of @sec-subdivided predicted this, and it is why `GD_WI_hyb`, the heterozygosity actually carried inside the F1s, is reported separately. And `GD_BS` *rises* under truncation: selection concentrates on the most complementary line pairs, which pushes the pools further apart. ::: {.callout-important} ## A blind optimiser erodes one pool while global $\theta$ looks fine Without this decomposition that goes unnoticed, and the consequence appears only in the following cycle. `ne_lines_pool()` is the cheap version of the same alarm -- it needs no `fL`, only the pedigree: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} t(sapply(sels, ne_lines_pool, ctx = ctx)) #> Ne_lines_A Ne_lines_B #> random 18.556701 20.93023 #> trunc_cap 15.517241 15.51724 #> greedy_w1 4.488778 11.84211 #> greedy_div 18.947368 18.36735 #> truncation 4.488778 11.84211 ``` ::: ### Where this could go next $\theta_A$, $\theta_B$ and $\theta_{AB}$ as computed here are **diagnostic**: reported, not fed back into the objective. The subdivided-population literature offers a ready-made way to promote them into a tunable target. @caballerorodriguezramilo2010, used by @lopezcortegano2019 to manage two heterotic-like pools simultaneously, partition total diversity as $$H_T = D_G + \lambda H_S, \qquad A_T = D_A + \lambda A_S,$$ where $H_S$ and $A_S$ are the within-pool components, $D_G$ and $D_A$ the between-pool components, and $\lambda \in [0, \infty)$ is a weight chosen by the breeder. $\lambda = 0$ optimises only between-pool divergence -- protects heterosis, ignores each pool's internal health. $\lambda \to \infty$ optimises only within-pool diversity -- protects each pool's future options, ignores the cross. That maps directly onto the two constraints a maize breeder already has in mind but applies only qualitatively: *don't blend the pools* versus *don't paint either pool into a corner*. Turning $\lambda$ into a second explicit knob alongside $\alpha_{\max}$ is the natural next step if pool erosion shows up in practice. The current implementation reports the ingredients and leaves the weighting to the analyst. $\lambda$ need not stay a matter of taste. @sec-heterosis shows that the value of between-pool divergence is not a free parameter but a $d$-weighted quantity: the divergence term contributes $\sum_k d_k y_k^2 / 2$ against the shared term's $\sum_k d_k \, 2\bar p_k (1 - \bar p_k)$. Given an estimate of the dominance deviations, the ratio of those two sums is what $\lambda$ is trying to express, and the reason a purely frequency-based partition cannot pin it down is that $d$ does not appear in the partition at all. ## The correct baseline {#sec-baseline} ### Why not compare against the whole population The natural comparison -- coancestry of the selected set against that of the whole population -- is **biased by construction**. Applying equation (1) to both: $$\theta_S - \theta_N = \left(\frac{1}{n} - \frac{1}{N}\right)\left(\bar f_d - \bar f_o\right) > 0,$$ since $\bar f_d > \bar f_o$ whenever individuals are not clones. A **random** sample already looks less diverse than the population it came from, with no selection whatsoever. The bias is pure sampling and grows as the sample shrinks. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fd <- mean(diag(ctx$f)); fo <- mean(ctx$f[upper.tri(ctx$f)]) predicted_bias <- (1 / n_sel - 1 / ctx$N) * (fd - fo) set.seed(11) observed_bias <- mean(replicate(400, theta_group(sample.int(ctx$N, n_sel), ctx))) - theta_group(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) c(predicted = predicted_bias, observed = observed_bias) #> predicted observed #> 0.002222092 0.002276690 ``` ::: The formula is exact; the residual is Monte Carlo error in the resampling. Note also that the **off-diagonal** mean of a random subset *is* an unbiased estimator of the population's off-diagonal mean. So the metric many programmes already use is free of this particular bias -- but it is also not comparable across sample sizes on the $N_s$ scale. ### Operational definition of loss The "0% loss" reference is the **distribution of random subsets of the same size**: $$\alpha \;=\; \frac{GD_{\text{random}(n)} - GD_S}{GD_{\text{random}(n)}}.$$ $\alpha = 0$ means "as diverse as a random sample of the same size"; $\alpha < 0$ means more diverse than chance. Resampling also delivers the standard deviation, and hence a z-score for any strategy. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} null <- null_distribution(ctx, n_sel, B = 400, B_full = 60) c(GD_population = gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx), GD_reference = null$gd_ref, sd = null$gd_sd, apparent_loss_if_wrong_baseline = (gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx) - null$gd_ref) / gene_diversity(seq_len(ctx$N), ctx)) #> GD_population GD_reference #> 0.3280928000 0.3258385719 #> sd apparent_loss_if_wrong_baseline #> 0.0007654486 0.0068707028 ``` ::: That last number is what a programme would report as a diversity loss if it compared against the full pool. It is entirely a sampling artefact. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} fmt(sapply(sels, alpha_loss, ctx = ctx, gd_ref = null$gd_ref), 5) #> random trunc_cap greedy_w1 greedy_div truncation #> 0.00032 0.00326 0.04122 -0.01352 0.04122 ``` ::: Negative values are selections *more* diverse than chance, which is exactly what the max-diversity greedy is for. ### How to set the $\alpha$ limit The acceptable limit **should not be chosen a priori.** Pure truncation -- the greediest possible selection -- defines the maximum attainable $\alpha$. If that ceiling is below your intended limit, the constraint restricts nothing and you have bought a false sense of control. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} attainable <- alpha_loss(sel_truncation(ctx, n_sel), ctx, null$gd_ref) c(attainable_alpha_max = attainable, intended_limit = 0.05, constraint_is_active = attainable > 0.05) #> attainable_alpha_max intended_limit constraint_is_active #> 0.04121618 0.05000000 0.00000000 ``` ::: At the full simulated scale that ceiling comes out near **3.6%**, so a 5% limit would be inoperative. The correct procedure is to trace the $\alpha$-versus-gain frontier and choose its knee, which is @sec-combinatorial. ## Every metric against the null A metric without a baseline says nothing. The z-score of each metric against the random-subset null is how this book reports all of them: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} tab <- evaluate(sels, ctx, null$gd_ref) fmt(as.data.frame(discriminatory_power(tab, null)[ , c("GD", "Ns", "Ne_parents", "F_hom", "F_drift", "alleles_lost", "ENE", "ANE")]), 1) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display}
| | GD| Ns| Ne_parents| F_hom| F_drift| alleles_lost| ENE| ANE| |:----------|-----:|-----:|----------:|-----:|-------:|------------:|----:|----:| |random | 0.0| 0.0| 1.4| 0.6| -1.2| 0.0| -1.0| -0.4| |trunc_cap | -1.3| -1.3| -2.7| 2.2| 3.1| 3.3| -0.7| 17.9| |greedy_w1 | -17.9| -17.6| -11.4| 9.5| 30.1| 14.9| -1.5| 10.2| |greedy_div | 6.1| 6.2| 0.4| -5.2| -0.7| -0.3| 5.5| 6.3| |truncation | -17.9| -17.6| -11.4| 9.5| 30.1| 14.9| -1.5| 10.2|
::: ::: Read the rows against each other. Truncation is many standard deviations from random on `F_drift` and on `Ne_parents` while being far less extreme on `GD` -- the constraint that would catch it is not the one most programmes apply. That observation is what @sec-choosing turns into a recommendation.
